heading: Lists and objects for custom elements
body:
A custom element is an element whose name has a dash, for example `w-chart` from a component library. When a binding on a custom element gives an object or an array, the page sets it as a JavaScript property of the element, not as an attribute. So `:data="stats.points"` gives the chart the array itself. The property name is the attribute name in camel case: `:chart-options` sets the property `chartOptions`. Text, numbers and `true` or `false` stay attributes, so the element can still watch them and CSS can still select them. Plain HTML elements, such as `div` or `input`, keep the attribute rules.

After an update the page writes the property again only when the value changed. A new array with the same values is not written again. A change inside the same array is not seen, so give the field a new array, for example `this.points = [...this.points, next]`. When the binding gives `null` or text again, the page sets the property to `undefined` and writes the attribute as before. The element's library can load after the page: the element gets the value through its own setter when it is defined. Functions are not passed to elements. An element can refuse a property, for example when it has a getter and no setter. Then the page skips that one binding, writes no attribute for it, and logs one console error that names the element and the binding; the rest of the page still renders. ADR 0136 records this rule.
